opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'm not sure "expected" is quite the right word. When Bill Peebles and I were working on DiT, I don't think either of us was sitting there thinking, "This is going to become the standard." It was more a feeling that something was a bit off in the field, and that we should test it.

At that time diffusion models were basically built on U-Nets. That made sense historically, because U-Net came from pixel-level prediction tasks like segmentation, and denoising looks a lot like that. But meanwhile the rest of deep learning had already moved to transformers. In language, in recognition, everywhere, people had seen that transformers scale very predictably: more compute, more parameters, and you just keep getting better. So the question we asked was pretty simple: is the U-Net's inductive bias actually essential for diffusion, or is it just a historical habit?

What we found was that it's mostly habit. If you work in a latent space, patchify it, and use a fairly standard Vision Transformer with a few careful design choices, like how you inject the timestep and class conditioning, the adaptive layer norm part, then you get a model that's simpler and scales really cleanly. The result I cared most about wasn't any single FID number. It was the scaling plot: as you increase the compute, quality improves very consistently. To me that's the signal that matters, because it means the architecture isn't going to be the bottleneck. You can just keep pushing.

So if I had any expectation, it was this: if the community really believes in scaling, sooner or later they'll want an architecture that behaves like the ones that already scale in other domains. And a transformer also unifies things. The same backbone, the same infrastructure, the same engineering knowledge from language models. That's very attractive to people who need to build big systems.

I should also say the reception wasn't immediate. The paper actually got rejected the first time we submitted it. Some reviewers felt it wasn't novel enough, basically "you just used a transformer." In a way I understand that, but I think it also shows a bias in how we judge research. Sometimes the most useful contribution isn't a clever new module. It's showing that something simpler and more general works, and works better as you scale. The adoption came later, when people started building large image and video generation systems and really needed that scalability. That's when it mattered.

r001.rationale: The response says a transformer unifies the backbone and infrastructure with language models, presenting that shared infrastructure as attractive.

r002.rationale: The response says adoption came later as people built large image and video generation systems, rather than saying the attention failed to produce actual adoption.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I didn't. When we wrote the DiT paper, the thinking in the community was that U-Nets were kind of sacred for diffusion. The inductive biases—the convolutions, the skip connections, the multi-scale structure—people believed those were essential to making diffusion work. So the paper was almost a contrarian exercise. Bill Peebles and I just wanted to ask a very simple question: is the U-Net actually necessary, or is it just historical accident?

And the answer we got was that the architecture didn't really matter in the way people assumed. What mattered was scale. If you take a plain transformer, treat the latent as a sequence of patches, and just scale it up—more compute, more parameters—the FID keeps going down in a very clean, predictable way. That scaling curve was the real result of the paper, more than the architecture itself.

Actually, the paper got rejected at CVPR the first time around. One of the reviews basically said it lacked novelty, that it was "just a transformer." Which, in a way, was the whole point. We weren't trying to invent something clever. We were trying to remove something that people thought they needed.

So if you're asking why I expected adoption, I think the honest answer is that I expected the opposite. I thought people would read it as a nice empirical study and move on. What changed things was that the field itself moved toward scaling. Once you believe scaling is the lever, you want the architecture that's the simplest, most well-understood, and best supported by the whole infrastructure built around language models. Transformers win on all those counts. So it wasn't that we convinced people; it was that the field converged on a worldview where DiT was the natural choice. Sora, Stable Diffusion 3—those came from that same conclusion, not from our paper being persuasive on its own.

I think there's a lesson in that for research generally. The good ideas often aren't the ones that look clever. They're the ones that remove complexity and happen to line up with where the whole field is going.

r001.rationale: The response says transformers are supported by language-model infrastructure, but does not clearly identify infrastructure sharing as a benefit of DiT’s architectural unification.

r002.rationale: The response does not say DiT received substantial attention without being adopted; it instead describes the field converging on DiT and names Sora and Stable Diffusion 3 as examples.

astra-6.text:
I think the expectation came from simplicity and scalability. With DiT, you could take a fairly standard transformer and use it as the backbone of a diffusion model. If you were already familiar with transformers, there wasn’t a completely new architecture you had to learn.

And the important part was that scaling it up worked. As we increased the model’s compute, sample quality improved. That gave researchers a clear direction: you could build on the architecture and take advantage of the tools and experience people already had with transformers.

So it wasn’t that I knew everyone would adopt it. It was more that a simple architecture with a convincing scaling trend seemed like something other researchers would want to explore.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main reason was simplicity. DiT takes the transformer architecture that researchers already know and applies it to diffusion. You don’t need a lot of specialized architectural choices—you turn the latent representation into patches and process them with transformer blocks.

That also makes it easy to build on improvements from the broader transformer ecosystem. And we showed a clear scaling trend: as you put more compute into the model, sample quality improves. So researchers had both a familiar starting point and a reason to believe that scaling it up would pay off.

r001.rationale: The response says DiT can build on improvements from the broader transformer ecosystem, but does not identify sharing infrastructure as a benefit of architectural unification.

r002.rationale: The response explains why researchers might adopt DiT; it does not say that substantial attention failed to translate into actual adoption.
